docs.title: Vector
docs.text:
State management for Roblox

Register typed state on players and models, react to updates, and replicate changes to clients in batches.

Get started Explore the API

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Results from a Roblox Studio server run comparing Vector's access classifier with ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache) and W-TinyLFU with a 4-bit sketch. The first three workloads score how well each method identifies hot fields. The fourth measures how many accesses it takes to promote a dormant field.

Scan pollution Vector100% ARC87.5% W-TinyLFU87.5% Exploration to combat Vector92.47% ARC89.6% W-TinyLFU20% Mixed update rates Vector100% ARC94.87% W-TinyLFU97.5%

The cards show the reported F1 scores on a 0–100% scale. F1 balances precision and recall. Higher scores indicate better hot-field classification, while lower delay indicates less measured work per access in this run.

docs.title: Scan pollution
docs.text:
A Zipfian workload followed by 20 one-off scan accesses. Vector classified all eight hot fields and all 20 cold fields correctly. ARC and W-TinyLFU each reported one false positive and one false negative.

docs.title: Exploration to combat
docs.text:
The working set switches from exploration to combat. Scores summarize 50 post-switch samples. Vector and ARC both reached 100% F1 at the final snapshot, while W-TinyLFU ended at 20%.

docs.title: Dormant field reactivation
docs.text:
This workload repeatedly accesses a dormant field against a saturated working set and records the access step where it is promoted to Fast.

Method Accesses to promotion Vector No promotion recorded ARC 1 W-TinyLFU 1

The run reports -1 for Vector, shown here as no promotion recorded.

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
These results describe one benchmark run. The final snapshot shows where each method ended, while the reported score reflects the scenario's sampling method. For example, the phase-switch score includes the transition period. Timing results describe the measured benchmark operations, not end-to-end network latency.

See Classification for how Vector computes velocity, acceleration, jerk, and alpha.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Set up the library as a ModuleScript named Vector in ReplicatedStorage. Use Vector/init.luau as the root module, with API, Config, VectorField, VectorTypes, Matrix, MatrixField, and UnsafeVector as child modules. Add a RemoteEvent named Shallow under the root module. To receive updates on clients, put Replicator.local.luau in StarterPlayerScripts as a LocalScript.

The server-side import waits for two Actors named exactly ParalleVector1 and ParalleVector2 under ServerScriptService, even when parallel writes are disabled. Create those Actors before requiring the API. For the serial example below, set Parallel = false and leave Experimental = false in Config. See Parallelism for the worker scripts.

Run this from a server Script after the player joins:

local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local Vector = require(ReplicatedStorage.Vector.API)

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    Vector.Init(player, {
        Health = { Value = 100, Type = "f32" },
        Stamina = { Value = 100 },
    })

    Vector.Write(player, {
        Health = { Value = 85, Type = "f32", Serial = true },
    })

    print(Vector.Read(player, "Health")) -- 85
end)

Pass the player or model instance to the public API. Player records are keyed by UserId. Model records use a CollectionService tag. The implementation takes the model's first returned tag as its key, so use a player for the first test and avoid relying on tag order for models with other tags.

For replication, the client listener needs the entity's initial Sync before it can apply a Batch for that entity.

docs.title: Listen
docs.text: The public signature is Vector.Listen(entity, options, target, callback, onExpire). Set options.Var to a registered field. If options.Type is omitted, the API selects "Poll". Only one listener entry is stored for each field, so a second registration replaces the stored entry.

docs.title: OnWrite
docs.text:
Vector.Listen(player, { Var = "Health", Type = "OnWrite" }, nil,
    function(entityId, fieldName, descriptor)
        print(entityId, fieldName, descriptor.Value)
    end
)

Vector.Write(player, {
    Health = { Value = 70, Type = "f32", Serial = true },
})

On the serial write path, the callback runs during the write and receives the write descriptor. It can run when the same value is written again. Keep the callback short because it runs inline.

docs.title: Poll with a target and deadline
docs.text:
Vector.Listen(player, {
    Var = "Health",
    Type = "Poll",
    Duration = 5,
}, 0, function(record)
    print("Health reached zero", record.Meta.UID)
end, function(record)
    print("Target was not reached", record.Meta.UID)
end)

Polling uses one shared Heartbeat connection. Each entry resolves the target, slow-map index, and expiry from its own entity record. The connection disconnects when the poll queue is empty. Fields classified as slow go through a counter check that can skip evaluation. See Information velocity for how fields are classified. A matching target or an expired deadline removes the poll entry. Duration is measured from listener registration, so it is a deadline rather than a timer that resets on writes. The callback and expiry callback receive the entity record. For a target match, pass a number or string such as 0 or "Ready".

"Event" connects directly to the remote's OnServerEvent. "Parallel" is experimental and needs the Actor setup. There is no separate "OnTimeout" mode or public unsubscribe handle.

docs.title: Matrices
docs.text:
A Matrix is an unowned entity table. It has its own name and groups shared scalars independently of any Roblox player or model. Writers identify themselves when updating a field, and a per-field lock decides which writer can apply the change.

Vector.Init(nil, {
    Matrix = true,
    Name = { Value = "Arena" },
    Round = { Value = 1 },
})

-- Use a player or registered model as the writer.
Vector.Write(player, {
    Target = "Arena",
    Round = { Value = 2 },
})

Matrix = true belongs alongside the fields in this example. Name.Value becomes the key in MatrixField. Declare the fields at initialization before writing to them. The write wrapper uses Target to look up the matrix and the entity ID to identify the writer. Check the spelling of the target. If it does not resolve to a matrix, the wrapper falls through to the ordinary entity write path.

For a server-side lookup, the internal module exposes Matrix.Read("Arena", "Round"). The public API.Read, Get, and Listen resolve entity state instead.

docs.title: Contended writes and ranking
docs.text:
Locks apply to individual fields. An unowned field grants its lock to the requesting writer. The owner can release the lock by calling the lock operation again. A competing writer initially receives "Locked" and increments the lock's attempt counter. Once the counter is greater than two, the next competing attempt can take ownership based on rank.

  • Explicit rank. Your game decides how to rank writers. The core function Vector.Rank(matrixId, writerId, rank) records the rank you supply. When both writers have explicit ranks, the contender must have a strictly higher rank than the current owner.
  • Velocity rank. If either writer lacks an explicit rank, the lock compares their velocity ranks. The contender must have a strictly lower velocity-rank value than the owner. Both values must be present for this comparison to grant ownership.

A successful takeover returns "Stolen" and resets the attempt counter. Matrix.Write applies the field update after either "Granted" or "Stolen", then releases the lock.

Matrix writes batch updates separately and schedule a flush after 0.5 seconds. Their batch encoder is called with compression disabled.

docs.title: Read
docs.text:
Call Vector.Read(entity, fieldName) with a registered player or model and an existing field name.

local health = Vector.Read(player, "Health")
print(health)

The reader decodes recognized numeric and vector buffers and returns an ordinary value directly if the field is already unpacked. Reads update access timing, so frequent reads can influence the field's velocity classification.

Initialize the entity and field before reading. Check the schema when you need to know whether a field exists.

docs.title: Inspecting multiple fields
docs.text:
local fields, entityId = Vector.Get(player)
print(entityId, fields.Health.Type)

Get returns a frozen shallow copy of the field table and the entity ID. The nested descriptors are shared, and their Value entries can contain buffers. Use Read for decoded values and Write for updates.

Use Type = "Bool" to read a packed boolean as the numeric value 0 or 1.

docs.title: Scalars
docs.text:
A scalar is one named value inside a Vector or Matrix. For example, Health is a scalar with the value 100. Its descriptor holds the value and its storage type.

Health = { Value = 100, Type = "f32" }

The name is the key in the parent table. If you omit Type, Vector infers it from Value. The term scalar describes one field in the state model. That field can also hold a Roblox value such as a Vector3.

Use Write to update a scalar, Read to retrieve it, and Listen to observe writes or poll for a target. See Classification for how access timing is tracked.

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text:
A Vector is an entity table that groups named scalars for a Roblox player or model. The entity gives the table its identity. Player Vectors use the player's UserId, and model Vectors use an entity tag.

Vector.Init(player, {
    Health = { Value = 100, Type = "f32" },
    Stamina = { Value = 80, Type = "f32" },
})

Here, the player owns the Vector and Health and Stamina are two scalars in that Vector. Pass the player to Write, Read, or Listen to work with those fields. For state shared independently of a player or model, use a Matrix.

Internally, the Vector record holds field descriptors, entity metadata, and access timing. See Records and data flow.

docs.title: Write
docs.text:
Vector.Write(entity, fields) accepts a player or model that has been registered with Vector.Init. Pass a table keyed by field name, with a descriptor for each field.

Vector.Write(player, {
    Health = { Value = 85.5, Type = "f32", Serial = true },
    Stamina = { Value = 70, Serial = true },
})
Descriptor key Effect Value The value to store. Type Optional encoding label. When omitted, the write uses typeof(Value), so repeat an explicit label such as "f32" on later writes. Serial Set to true to skip the parallel write branch for this field. Critical Recorded when a field is added. During initialization, critical descriptors are also placed in the rollback table.

On the serial path, updating an existing field updates its access timing, invokes its OnWrite listener, and queues a replication record. The first queued write schedules a flush after 0.5 seconds. Later writes can join that batch. A write can add a missing field, but declaring fields in Init gives them a timestamp slot up front.

Use the keyed form even for a single field. Target is a special top-level key used for matrix writes. Ordinary writes should omit it.

docs.title: Records and data flow
docs.text:
The public API module resolves Roblox instances to entity IDs. The root Vector module uses those IDs to manage records in VectorField. The client replicator also uses VectorField, but the client has its own copy. MatrixField holds a separate set of named records.

Record member Contents Data Descriptors keyed by field name. Each descriptor stores Value and Type, and may have flags such as Critical or Encoded. Meta Record identity, field indices, access timing, listener entries, and flags such as Valid and Compact. Prev Descriptors saved during registration for fields marked Critical.

docs.title: Registration and identity
docs.text:
API.Init accepts either a field table or a wrapper with a Data member. The root module fills in missing type labels using typeof, registers the record, serializes its values, and builds the timestamp bitmap for ordinary entity records. Registration uses the player's UserId or the model's first CollectionService tag as the lookup key. For matrices, the key is Name.Value and registration uses a different metadata layout.

The registration path also broadcasts Sync. This is the snapshot the client needs before it can apply later batches. See Compression and replication for the wire format and delivery behavior.

docs.title: Serial reads and writes
docs.text:
On a read, Vector resolves the descriptor, decompresses the local value if required, and decodes recognized buffer types. It also updates record-level access times, evaluates field timing, and stores the field's latest timestamp.

On a serial write, Vector replaces the existing field's value and type, or creates a descriptor and appends the field name to Meta.IDs. An existing field also goes through velocity evaluation and timestamp recording. The write then updates the listener's cached value, calls an inline OnWrite callback when present, and queues a replication entry. The call serializes the record if it was marked noncompact and schedules a batch flush if one is pending for the first time.

Get freezes a shallow clone of the field table. Its descriptors still reference the original data. Mutating one directly can bypass timestamp updates, listeners, and batch queuing.

docs.title: Listener ownership
docs.text: The serial write path updates the listener entry under the entity's Meta.Listening[fieldName]. The shared Heartbeat connection walks PollT. Each poll entry supplies its entity ID and field name, and the loop resolves its target, field index, and expiry from that entity. See Listen for callback arguments and deadline examples.

docs.title: Rollback and matrix locks
docs.text:
Rollback deserializes a record, copies entries from Prev into Data, then serializes again. The global form iterates through VectorField.

A matrix write takes a separate route through Matrix.Write. Its lock records live in Meta.Dot and are keyed by field. The matrix uses its own batch and encoder. See Matrices for the contention rules, caller-defined ranks, and velocity-rank fallback.

docs.title: Compression and replication
docs.text:
Vector uses buffers for field values and separately packs access timestamps. The value format depends on the descriptor's type label.

Value Buffer format Number labeled f32 Rounded to two decimal places, then written as a four-byte float. Other numbers Eight-byte float. The decoder recognizes number and f64. Vector3 Three four-byte floats at offsets 0, 4, and 8. Boolean One byte with 0 or 1. The byte decoder checks for the label Bool.

docs.title: Storage encoding
docs.text:
Serialize walks record.Data, converts supported values into buffers, and marks the record compact. It skips tables and existing buffers. For Vector3 fields it reads components from descriptor.Value. Deserialize reverses recognized encodings in place and clears the record's compact flag. Read instead decodes a local value for one field.

When Alpha > 0.4, Compress attempts Zstd compression for fields in the slow map and sets each compressed descriptor's Encoded flag. The current compression pass skips descriptors already flagged as encoded. Read decompresses its local buffer before decoding, so the stored bytes and flag stay together during that operation.

docs.title: Replication messages
docs.text:
Operation Payload and client behavior Sync Registration broadcasts a record through Shallow. The client stores it by entity ID and deserializes its fields. Batch The server sends a list of updates. Each entry carries UID, Index (the field name), Data, and Type, plus Compressed when set by the batch encoder. The client applies updates only to records already present in its field table. Correction The handler receives a field name and descriptor and assigns that descriptor to the client record.

A serial write queues the input value for replication separately from the stored descriptor. The first write schedules a flush after 0.5 seconds. Subsequent writes join that batch until it is sent and the queue is reset. The normal Vector flush calls Serde(batch, true) before broadcasting; matrix writes use a separate queue and call their encoder with compression disabled.

The wire flag Compressed belongs to a batch entry, whereas Encoded belongs to a stored descriptor. The batch decoder decompresses when Compressed is set, then decodes recognized buffer types.

The client uses the initial snapshot to identify the entity and its fields when applying later updates.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text: Vector measures the timing of accesses to a field. It does not compare the old and new field values when classifying a field. Reads and updates to existing fields evaluate velocity before recording a fresh field timestamp.

docs.title: Field indices and timestamp layout
docs.text:
Meta.IDs maps numeric slots to field names. The bitmap builder allocates 36-byte groups. The first four bytes form a 32-bit occupancy mask, and the next 32 bytes provide one timestamp byte per field. BitIndex selects a group using ceil(fieldId / 32).

tick = floor(time / resolution) % 256

For the first four fields in a group, the timestamp word begins at byte offset 4. Each field uses a different shift within that word: 0, 8, 16, or 24 bits. TimeBit reads the word, clears that slot with a mask, and inserts the new tick. Because the stored tick wraps every 256 steps, a timestamp byte alone does not tell you the absolute time.

docs.title: Resolution and timing samples
docs.text: CycleTime uses elapsed os.clock() time and the current resolution to update the record's cycle counter. Resolution derives a new resolution from the precision of a timing value based on Meta.LastUpdate. Velocity calculations use both the resolution and the cycle counter to scale the quantized times.

docs.title: Velocity
docs.text:
A scalar's velocity sample describes the timing of its accesses. On a read or an update to an existing field, Vector compares the current quantized time with the field's previous timestamp before recording the new access.

velocity = abs(currentTime - previousFieldTime) / (currentTime + resolution / 10)

The denominator scales the difference relative to the current time estimate. The resolution term keeps the denominator positive near zero. This gives each field a timing sample that can be compared with the same entity's reference. For example, repeatedly reading Health can change its classification even if its value stays at 100.

docs.title: Acceleration
docs.text:
Acceleration describes changes in the entity's access timing. The sampler computes a velocity-like delta using the entity's last update time as its reference, then stores the sample in Meta.Snapshots.Velocity. Every pair of samples produces one acceleration value:

acceleration = abs(newVelocity - previousVelocity)
               / (previousVelocity + resolution / 10)

The sampler clears the velocity pair after using it and appends the result to Meta.Snapshots.Acceleration. Similar timing samples produce a small acceleration. A larger difference relative to the previous sample produces a larger one.

docs.title: Jerk
docs.text:
Once two acceleration samples are available, Vector measures how much acceleration changed and records the direction of that change.

direction = newAcceleration - previousAcceleration
jerk = abs(direction) / (previousAcceleration + resolution / 10)

Direction retains the sign. Jerk measures the size of the change relative to the previous acceleration. Vector stores both values on the entity and clears the acceleration samples so the next pair can be collected.

docs.title: Alpha
docs.text:
Alpha sets how much weight the current timing reference gets. Until jerk and direction are available, the function returns 0.4. After that it normalizes the two signals, combines them, and bounds the result:

normalizedJerk = jerk / (jerk + resolution / 10)
normalizedDirection = direction / (direction + resolution)
alpha = clamp(abs(normalizedJerk + normalizedDirection), 0.1, 0.9)

An alpha of 0.1 gives the current timing term 10% of the weight and the previous reference 90%. An alpha of 0.9 reverses those weights. Vector applies the timing scale after blending and compares the smoothed result with the current entity reference to compute Meta.DeltaRV. The current reference is the mean of the entity's quantized last update and the reference timestamp found by scanning its fields.

When Vector calculates alpha from samples, it also invokes the adaptive compression path. That path uses alpha and the slow map to select stored values. See Compression and replication.

docs.title: Fast and slow fields
docs.text:
The classifier compares the access delta against Meta.DeltaRV with a gate of 0.4 * resolution. A delta above the upper bound marks the field slow, a delta below the lower bound marks it fast, and a delta between the bounds preserves its previous classification. The maps use numeric field IDs as keys and field names as values.

The polling loop resolves the field name in the current entity's Meta.IDs before checking that entity's slow map. Slow entries go through an additional counter check that can skip evaluation. The shared counter and Heartbeat scheduling do not imply a fixed sampling frequency.

docs.title: Parallelism
docs.text: Vector has a serial write path and an optional Actor dispatch branch. Start with the serial path when integrating the library. Set Parallel = false in Config, or set Serial = true on every descriptor in a write that must stay on the serial path.

docs.title: Actor layout
docs.text:
ServerScriptService/
  ParalleVector1/      Actor
    ActorScript        Script
    Unsafe             ModuleScript
  ParalleVector2/      Actor
    ActorScript        Script
    Unsafe             ModuleScript

Use ActorScript.legacy.luau and Unsafe.luau as the sources for each Actor's children. The spelling in the tree matches UnsafeVector.luau. On the server, that module waits for both Actors at import time independently of the Parallel setting.

docs.title: Dispatch and reconciliation
docs.text: When parallel writes are enabled and a descriptor does not specify Serial, CheckRate compares the current timing delta with a smoothed threshold. If the threshold is crossed, UnsafeVector.Distribute sends a Write message to the Actor with the lower tracked work count. The Actor scripts include Sync and res messages, and the Unsafe.Serial path reconciles returned descriptors into the entity's field table and invokes applicable write listeners.

docs.title: Write gate and worker counters
docs.text:
The gate in CheckRate uses a resolution of 0.1 seconds and compares the quantized current time with Vector.GlobalUpdate. Once Vector.Delay has been initialized, the gate blends the current delta with the stored delta using weights of 0.4 and 0.6. Dispatch is attempted only when the current delta exceeds that gate. This calculation uses global access timing, whereas the fast and slow maps use each entity's field timestamps.

Distribute increments the selected worker's Work counter and picks the first worker on a tie. The root module subtracts the counts returned by the reconciliation calls. Those counts describe reconciled descriptors and are not measurements of CPU utilization.

docs.title: Message flow
docs.text:
Message Role in the current code Write Carries the entity ID and a descriptor with its field index. The Actor handler passes it to UnsafeWrite. Sync Carries staged writes to the Actor's message handler, which sends them back as res. res The serial handler stores the returned writes and calls Unsafe.Serial to apply them to the field table. Listen, Sound, Call Carry experimental listener registrations, match checks, and match results.

Reconciliation assigns descriptors to the live record, refreshes the listener's cached value, and invokes its inline OnWrite callback when present. The send and the serial reconciliation call do not form a blocking request and response. A read immediately after dispatch can still see the previous value.
